en.title: In-Process 16th October 2026
en.summary: We’ve got a bumper edition for you this week, with new content for just about everyone! Accessibility Testing with NVDA NV Access Survey New Help Options for NVDA Users Help for Low Vision Users Free Sample Accessibility Testing with NVDA NVDA 2026.3 Beta 5 Accessibility Testing with NVDA NV Access is very pleased to announce… Read More
en.body:
We’ve got a bumper edition for you this week, with new content for just about everyone!

NV Access is very pleased to announce the release of a new training package. Accessibility Testing with NVDA is designed for people using NVDA to test apps and websites for accessibility.

This Accessibility Testing with NVDA package includes: A training module with over 60 topics in nine sections Getting Started Setting up NVDA Reading information Visual Options Keyboard navigation Navigating content with NVDA Working with elements Testing with a screen reader Reporting Issues A printable NVDA Reference Sheet, with the commands most useful for accessibility testing A printable guide to writing accessible content on a single, printable sheet for easy consultation A list of NV Access and external resources and links to further your knowledge A WCAG 2.2 Reference with tips on testing many of the criteria with NVDA A JPG Badge you can proudly display in your email, or on your website or elsewhere to indicate your support

The purchase price of the module is A$250 (+GST for Australian buyers). Not only do you get a wealth of accessibility testing information, the cost of this package also supports the work of NV Access and helps continue our ability to provide the NVDA screen reading software free of charge.

Please note that this package is useable by both sighted and screen reader users. It is aimed at professionals wanting to test websites, documents and programs for accessibility. If you would like to learn to use NVDA from scratch as a blind or low vision screen reader user, please first consider “ Basic Training for NVDA ” or the “ NVDA Productivity Bundle “.

The Accessibility Testing with NVDA module is designed to teach you to incorporate NVDA into your accessibility testing workflow. It is not intended to replace dedicated accessibility testing tools which can give specific information about testing criteria and compliance etc. If you would like more formal training specifically in web accessibility, we recommend Learn.Intopia.digital . Intopia provided feedback on the web accessibility components of this material.

Please head to Accessibility Testing with NVDA to read more and purchase the new package.

Cover image of “Accessibility Testing with NVDA”

The NVDA Satisfaction Survey 2026 is open, but only until early next week.

We are always interested in understanding the satisfaction of our NVDA users, what is important to you & what we can do more effectively. The survey is anonymous & we encourage you to leave comments in your response.

We’re interested in hearing from as many people as possible, so please feel free to pass this on to others.

The survey is short, only three questions – we deliberately do that in order to make it less onerous to fill out. The rating is a simple, and industry standard metric (a “net promoter score”) we can use to benchmark broadly how well we are doing compared to previous years. We leave room for you to add your own thoughts, so you can give feedback on that one specific point on your mind. If you want a response, please do include your email address as we don’t otherwise collect contact details.

We do sometimes get questions like “It would be great if NVDA had feature X” and it’s frustrating to not be able to reply, especially when NVDA does in fact have feature X, but we have no way to reach the person to share that with them. We have also been asked “Why don’t you ask more questions about X, Y, or Z?” – which is a great question. This survey is designed to collect feedback on everything overall, and we try to keep it fairly consistent from year to year. We do conduct specific surveys from time to time, both more formally, and occasionally just a simple question on Mastodon asking, “What do you think about …”. We like to think we are approachable and easy to get in contact with, so do please always reach out if there is something you’d like to give feedback on or to ask.

Please do head over to https://www.nvaccess.org/survey2026 and fill out the survey if you haven’t already.

We are always looking for ways to help users and make more information available, and easy to find. For many years, the navbar of the NV Access website has had a “Get Help” option. This has linked to a single page of really useful information for NVDA users , including the training material, user groups, how to report an issue or get extra voices, and an FAQ. Now, we have expanded it to a menu. The first item lets you get help for “NVDA Users” and is the original “Get Help” item.

There are also several new options, which are covered below:

With the release of the magnifier in NVDA 2026.2, it seemed a good time to collate some of the features and settings in NVDA which can be useful for low vision users. The way low vision users will have NVDA setup may be different to how a totally blind user who does not use the screen may have it setup. This “ Get Help for Low Vision Users ” page includes information about: The magnifier: including a demo video, list of keystrokes, and link to the comparison with Windows Magnifier we did here in In-Process. Visual Highlighter: How to turn it on and just what the different colours mean. How to reduce speech: Turning on or off individual elements, or adjusting the speech mode overall. Working on the Web: Tips for navigating web pages, and copying information from the web. Other Windows Settings: Suggestions for other Windows settings which can be useful for low vision users.

To go with the brand-new Accessibility Testing with NVDA package , we have made a free sample of the material available. This extensive sample is full of web accessibility tips and tricks with the world’s favourite free screen reader, and is still only a small taste of the full product.

Do check out the Accessibility Testing with NVDA sample page in the new revamped “Get Help” menu. If you find it useful, you will find even more in the full Accessibility Testing with NVDA package , plus you will be supporting us to keep NVDA available for free to everyone who can use it.

Once again, our thanks to Intopia.Digital for their ongoing support of NV Access.

Finally, this week, we’re now up to Beta 5 of NVDA 2026.3 . Last In-Process we were up to Beta 2, so here’s what’s been in the latest three updates:

Changes introduced in Beta 5: Updates to translations Added bug fix for NVDA failing to start on Windows versions older than Windows 10 1903

Changes introduced in Beta 4: Updates to translations Added bug fix for lag in the Add-on Store when searching using Chinese characters Minor documentation changes

Changes introduced in Beta 3: Updates to translations Reverted bug fix to terminals, meaning NVDA may freeze again when substantial amounts of text are dumped to the screen. This is due to the bug fix not working correctly Prevented Magnifier crash recovery from flashing to reduce seizure risk

That’s all for this week. It’s not often the latest beta gets bumped to the SIXTH article in the blog! That by no means reflects on its value though – Please do try NVDA 2026.3 Beta 5 if you haven’t already. If you do any web accessibility work, please do check out the new Accessibility Testing with NVDA Package . It will be around release time for NVDA 2026.3 by next edition, so we’ll have more on the new version. And we’ll also cover a bit more for our low vision users as well.

es.title: Un nuevo prototipo busca llevar el Braille electrónico a restaurantes museos y puntos de información
es.summary: Un equipo de estudiantes de Shawnee State University ha desarrollado una línea Braille electrónica actualizable para facilitar el acceso a la información en espacios públicos. El proyecto continúa en desarrollo y sus creadores trabajan para mejorar el dispositivo y reducir sus costes de fabricación. Una línea Braille para consultar información en espacios públicos Dos estudiantes […] La entrada Un nuevo prototipo busca llevar el Braille electrónico a restaurantes museos y puntos de información se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Un equipo de estudiantes de Shawnee State University ha desarrollado una línea Braille electrónica actualizable para facilitar el acceso a la información en espacios públicos. El proyecto continúa en desarrollo y sus creadores trabajan para mejorar el dispositivo y reducir sus costes de fabricación.

Dos estudiantes de Ingeniería Informática y Tecnologías de Computación de Shawnee State University, en Estados Unidos, han creado un prototipo de línea Braille electrónica que podría facilitar el acceso a información en lugares como restaurantes, museos y puntos de información.

Los estudiantes Parker Lauders y Kade Dancy desarrollaron el dispositivo como proyecto final de sus estudios universitarios. Su objetivo es ofrecer una alternativa a los materiales en Braille impresos, especialmente en espacios donde la información cambia con frecuencia.

La propuesta utiliza tecnología Braille actualizable. En lugar de recurrir a textos impresos de forma permanente, el dispositivo emplea puntos mecánicos que suben y bajan para representar diferentes caracteres. Así, el contenido puede modificarse electrónicamente sin tener que producir un nuevo material en relieve cada vez que cambia la información.

Uno de los ejemplos que plantean sus creadores es el de los restaurantes. Los menús pueden cambiar varias veces al año, por lo que mantenerlos disponibles en Braille requiere actualizar e imprimir nuevos materiales.

Con una pantalla electrónica como esta, el establecimiento podría cargar el contenido actualizado en el dispositivo. De este modo, las personas ciegas podrían consultar la información en Braille sin depender exclusivamente de cartas impresas que pueden quedarse desactualizadas.

La misma idea podría aplicarse a museos, quioscos informativos y otros espacios públicos en los que se ofrecen datos sobre servicios, exposiciones o indicaciones.

El planteamiento busca que la información accesible sea más fácil de mantener y actualizar. No obstante, su utilidad real dependerá de cómo se implemente el sistema en cada entorno y de que el contenido esté disponible en un formato adecuado para las personas usuarias.

La idea surgió cuando Parker Lauders era estudiante de primer año. Tras varios años de formación práctica, él y Kade Dancy consiguieron diseñar, construir y programar un prototipo funcional como parte de su proyecto final.

El trabajo combina componentes electrónicos, programación y piezas mecánicas fabricadas específicamente para el dispositivo. Según la documentación académica del proyecto, el sistema incorpora 20 celdas Braille personalizadas y un microcontrolador STM32.

Aunque el proyecto ha permitido desarrollar y probar distintos componentes del sistema, todavía existen aspectos técnicos que deben mejorarse, especialmente en el mecanismo encargado de accionar los puntos Braille.

Por ello, sus creadores continúan trabajando en el hardware, la funcionalidad y la reducción de los costes de fabricación. También prevén explorar la protección mediante patente y las posibilidades de llevar la tecnología al mercado.

El proyecto se ha presentado en el Capitolio del Estado de Ohio, una oportunidad para mostrar su potencial más allá del entorno universitario.

Por el momento, no se ha anunciado que el dispositivo esté disponible comercialmente . Se trata de un prototipo universitario en fase de desarrollo, no de un producto que pueda comprarse e instalarse actualmente en restaurantes o museos.

Su evolución será interesante para el ámbito de la accesibilidad, ya que plantea una posible forma de facilitar la actualización de información en Braille en espacios públicos.

Si consigue resolver los retos técnicos pendientes y alcanzar un coste de fabricación asumible, podría abrir nuevas posibilidades para que establecimientos y entidades ofrezcan información accesible de manera más flexible.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

en.title: From Word to Teams: Using ZoomText and Fusion Across Your Workday
en.summary: ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech. Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful …
en.body:
ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech.

Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful features of ZoomText and Fusion that will help you be more productive in the workplace. This blog series will run throughout October, with a new post every Thursday featuring helpful information and practical tips to make the most of ZoomText and Fusion as you work.

For many professionals, the workday is a journey through Microsoft Office and a variety of collaboration tools. Whether you’re writing, analyzing data, managing emails, or joining virtual meetings, having ZoomText or Fusion set up to support your workflow can make all the difference. This week, we’ll look at how these tools can help you work more efficiently and comfortably, from your first document to your last video call.

Drafting reports or editing proposals is easier when you can see exactly what you need. With ZoomText, you can quickly adjust your magnification level or switch between different zoom window types—like Lens or Line view—to focus on the text that matters most. For longer documents, AppReader is a helpful feature: just press CAPS LOCK+ALT+A to have the text read aloud, letting you follow along visually or simply listen and rest your eyes.

Fusion users can also take advantage of JAWS navigation commands, such as jumping between headings or moving by paragraph, to quickly scan and organize content. To jump by heading, first turn on Quick Navigation keys by pressing CAPS LOCK+Z , then press H to navigate forward through headings or SHIFT+H to navigate backward. Press P to navigate forward by paragraph and SHIFT+P to navigate backward. Press CAPS LOCK+Z to toggle Quick Navigation keys off again so you can continue editing your document.

Keyboard Echo is another useful feature, giving you spoken feedback as you type, so you can be sure your edits are accurate.

To cycle through the different Keyboard Echo settings, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+K . The setting No Echo disables all keyboard echo. Keys will echo your keystrokes as you type. Words will echo individual words as you type them. And Keys and Words will echo both keystrokes and words as you type.

Spreadsheets can be intimidating, but ZoomText’s magnification tools help you zero in on the data you need. Adjust your zoom to see more or less of your sheet and use Reading Zones to mark important areas—like totals or headers—so you can return to them instantly.

A reading zone is a defined area of an application window that ZoomText can display, speak, or both, at the press of a hotkey. To create a reading zone, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+C , then drag a rectangle over the area of the application window you want the zone to cover. To trigger a reading zone, press CAPS LOCK+ALT+ the zone’s number (1 through 9, or 0 for zone 10).

Fusion users can rely on JAWS table navigation to move efficiently through rows and columns, with commands like CAPS LOCK+C to read the current cell, helping you keep your place in complex data.

Staying on top of emails and appointments is simple with the right tools. AppReader lets you listen to long emails, while Focus Enhancements in ZoomText highlight your current selection, making it easier to track where you are.

AppReader reads documents, web pages, and email aloud while you follow along or rest your eyes. It can read from beginning to end, skim forward and backward, or read just the text you select with the mouse. AppReader reads text aloud in three modes: App View reads directly in the source application without changing your view, Text View reformats the text with your choice of fonts, colors, and magnification for easier reading, and the SpeakIt Tool reads any text on the screen that you select by clicking and dragging. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+A to launch App View. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+T to launch Text View. Press CAPS LOCK+ALT+S to launch the SpeakIt Tool.

Focus enhancements highlight the item you are on as you navigate using the Tab and arrow keys through menus, dialogs, and toolbars, making it easy to keep your place. Press CAPS LOCK+F to toggle focus enhancements on and off.

Fusion users can use commands like CTRL+N to create a new message, CTRL+R to reply to a message, or CTRL+F to forward a message. You can also switch to different areas in Outlook with quick shortcuts like CTRL+1 to go to your current mail folder, CTRL+2 to navigate to the calendar, and CTRL+3 to go to Contacts.

Whether you’re building slides or presenting to your team, ZoomText’s flexible magnification ensures you can see every detail. AppReader can read slide content aloud, making it easier to review your work or follow along during a presentation. Fusion users can use the arrow keys with JAWS to navigate slides and read speaker notes, so you’re always prepared and in control. Press F6 in PowerPoint to navigate the different areas of your presentation.

Today’s workplace relies on video conferencing apps like Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and Google Meet. With ZoomText and Fusion, you can adjust your magnification to follow chat messages, participant panels, and shared screens during meetings. AppReader and JAWS speech help you keep up with notifications and chat without missing a beat.

A standout feature for video calls is Face-in-View . Before joining a meeting, open the Face-in-View tool in Fusion by pressing INSERT+SPACE, F , then O . This feature uses your webcam to show you a live preview and provides feedback to help you center your face and check your lighting—so you can join every call looking your best and feeling confident.

Join us next week as we explore how ZoomText and Fusion can help you access more online, making web browsing and digital resources easier and more accessible. Stay tuned for more tips to help you thrive in your workplace!

Have questions? Email training@vispero.com .

With the right setup and a few helpful features, ZoomText and Fusion can empower you to work smarter and more comfortably, every step of the way.

es.title: SparkVision Glasses 2: un nuevo modelo de gafas con IA para ceguera y baja visión
es.summary: Las nuevas gafas asistivas de SparkVision leen etiquetas, describen entornos y responden a preguntas mediante inteligencia artificial. Hay dos versiones disponibles, con precios desde 1.500 euros. Las gafas inteligentes con inteligencia artificial siguen ganando terreno en el ámbito de la accesibilidad visual. Una de las propuestas más recientes es SparkVision Glasses 2, una familia de […] La entrada SparkVision Glasses 2: un nuevo modelo de gafas con IA para ceguera y baja visión se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Las nuevas gafas asistivas de SparkVision leen etiquetas, describen entornos y responden a preguntas mediante inteligencia artificial. Hay dos versiones disponibles, con precios desde 1.500 euros.

Las gafas inteligentes con inteligencia artificial siguen ganando terreno en el ámbito de la accesibilidad visual. Una de las propuestas más recientes es SparkVision Glasses 2 , una familia de gafas diseñadas para ayudar a las personas ciegas y con baja visión a acceder a información visual mediante respuestas habladas.

La empresa búlgara SparkVision ha presentado esta nueva generación en demostraciones presenciales y eventos tecnológicos durante septiembre de 2026. Sin embargo, hay una diferencia importante respecto a otras novedades del sector: las gafas ya aparecen a la venta en la tienda oficial de la compañía .

La gama incluye dos versiones, con diferentes prestaciones y precios. Según la tienda oficial, ambas se comercializan con IVA incluido.

Ambas versiones incluyen el anillo inteligente SparkVision Smart Ring, que permite controlar funciones sin tener que manipular continuamente las gafas.

La compañía ofrece información de compra en su tienda oficial . También indica que realiza envíos a los países de la Unión Europea cuando existe disponibilidad para la dirección o modalidad de entrega seleccionada.

No obstante, antes de comprar desde España conviene confirmar el plazo de entrega, las condiciones de envío y las prestaciones incluidas en cada paquete.

El objetivo de SparkVision Glasses 2 es convertir información visual en respuestas habladas. Para ello, incorporan una cámara, micrófonos y un sistema de control integrado en la montura.

Estas son algunas de sus funciones principales.

Las gafas pueden reconocer textos impresos y reproducirlos mediante voz. Esta función puede ser útil para consultar cartas de restaurantes, envases, etiquetas de productos, recibos y documentos cotidianos.

También ofrecen lectura de varias páginas y herramientas para facilitar el posicionamiento de los textos frente a la cámara.

Otra de las funciones anunciadas es la descripción del entorno. El usuario puede obtener información hablada sobre lo que aparece delante de la cámara y utilizar el asistente para preguntar sobre una escena.

El sistema también incorpora una función para buscar objetos. El usuario indica qué quiere localizar y recibe orientación hablada para encontrarlo dentro del campo de visión.

Estas posibilidades pueden facilitar algunas tareas cotidianas, aunque las respuestas de la inteligencia artificial pueden ser incorrectas o incompletas.

Las gafas también incluyen herramientas para identificar colores, detectar luz y reconocer billetes.

La versión Ultra añade funciones como el recuento estimado de dinero visible y la lectura de información presente en los recibos. Como sucede con otros sistemas de reconocimiento visual, es importante comprobar los resultados antes de realizar pagos o tomar decisiones económicas.

SparkVision Glasses 2 incorpora un asistente de IA para responder preguntas y ofrecer información sobre el entorno.

Además, permite iniciar una llamada a una persona de confianza previamente elegida. Durante esa llamada, el usuario puede compartir la perspectiva de la cámara para recibir ayuda humana cuando la inteligencia artificial no sea suficiente.

La posibilidad de recurrir a una persona es especialmente interesante en situaciones en las que una descripción automática no proporciona toda la información necesaria.

La diferencia entre las dos versiones no se limita al precio.

SparkVision Glasses 2 Ultra incorpora funciones adicionales de orientación y acceso a información durante los desplazamientos. Entre ellas se encuentran la navegación asistida y la consulta de información sobre transporte público, como paradas, líneas y salidas.

También incluye una batería externa que, según el fabricante, permite alcanzar hasta 12 horas de uso, dependiendo de las condiciones y del modo utilizado. La versión Lite anuncia hasta cuatro horas de uso activo.

El equipo pesa aproximadamente 38,5 gramos, según las especificaciones técnicas publicadas por SparkVision. La cámara integrada tiene una resolución de 12 megapíxeles y la conectividad incluye Wi-Fi 6 y Bluetooth 5.3.

No todas las funciones dependen necesariamente de la nube, pero tampoco conviene afirmar que las gafas funcionan completamente sin Internet.

El manual oficial explica que determinados procesos se realizan localmente, mientras que otros utilizan la aplicación SparkVision Assistant y los servicios de la compañía. Las funciones en línea pueden transmitir datos a los servicios de SparkVision o a proveedores de procesamiento.

La aplicación complementaria está destinada a Android, según la documentación técnica. Por eso, antes de adquirirlas, conviene comprobar la compatibilidad con el teléfono y las funciones que requieren conexión o acceso adicional.

Las gafas de inteligencia artificial pueden facilitar el acceso a información visual, pero es importante conocer sus límites.

SparkVision advierte en su manual que el dispositivo no debe utilizarse como único apoyo para desplazarse en entornos peligrosos. Tampoco debe confiarse exclusivamente en sus respuestas para cruzar calles, acercarse a vehículos o tomar decisiones relacionadas con la seguridad.

Estas herramientas deben entenderse como un complemento a los apoyos habituales de movilidad y accesibilidad, no como un sustituto del bastón blanco, del perro guía o de las técnicas de orientación y movilidad.

También es recomendable tener en cuenta la privacidad. Las gafas incorporan cámara y micrófonos, por lo que su utilización debe respetar la intimidad de las personas y las normas aplicables a la captación de imágenes y sonido.

La propuesta de SparkVision destaca por reunir lectura de textos, reconocimiento de objetos, descripción de escenas y asistencia mediante IA en un dispositivo portátil.

La versión Lite ofrece un conjunto de funciones básicas por 1.500 euros, mientras que la Ultra amplía las posibilidades de orientación y transporte público por 5.566 euros. La diferencia de precio es considerable, por lo que conviene comparar las necesidades de cada usuario con las funciones realmente incluidas.

Por ahora, la información oficial confirma que las dos versiones forman parte de la oferta comercial de SparkVision , aunque la disponibilidad concreta y los plazos de entrega deben comprobarse durante el proceso de compra.

Para las personas ciegas y con baja visión interesadas en nuevas herramientas de asistencia visual, estas gafas son una opción que merece seguimiento, especialmente por la combinación de lectura, descripción del entorno y posibilidad de contactar con una persona de confianza.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes consultadas: Spark Vision Tienda , ficha técnica del producto , manual de usuario , demostraciones presenciales

es.title: Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 5 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 5 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 5 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es c1d2cc7bc21126a224fdc0733fef5f20adf212d6098fd31863c89f7d05195544. ¡Feliz miércoles!

La entrada Ya disponible la quinta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.title: Welcome Home: Apple Announces Updated HomePod Mini, Apple TV, All-New HomeView, and New Home Accessories
en.summary: Apple today announced updated models of the HomePod Mini and Apple TV 4K ; as well as an all-new HomeView smart home hub and a collection of smart home accessories . HomePod Mini 2 Powered by the S10 chip and what Apple calls "advanced computational audio," up to four HomePod Mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers can be paired to create a surround sound experience with the new Apple TV 4K. Siri AI will be available on HomePod Mini 2 with a future software update. It can recognize up to six people in a household, and can use a user's Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad to draw on their personal context. With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod Mini 2 can glow and pulse in sync with the currently playing song. Users can additionally customize the displayed animations to promote a relaxing atmosphere. HomePod Mini 2 features 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets, and 100 percent recycled copper, gold plating, and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today in pink, green, blue, white and midnight for US $149, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, October 30. HomeView HomeView is a smart home hub with a speaker and 7-inch display, which can either be placed on a table or mounted on a wall. It features a variety of Apple apps and widgets on the Home Screen, and allows users to play music, view photos and videos, make and receive FaceTime calls, monitor and control their home, and more using Siri or the touch interface. HomeView can display a generic screen for everyone in the household, or recognize up to six faces to show personalized content for individual users. Apple Silicon and HomeView's speaker array can optimize audio for loudness and bass response at any volume, with tailored profiles for the table-top and wall-mounted models. Siri AI can be used to play media on HomeView, answer general knowledge questions, discuss recipes, and if a user has an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad, draw on their personal context for more helpful responses. Like other Apple Intelligence-capable devices, conversations with Siri AI on HomeView are synced via iCloud and viewable in the Siri app on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. Changes made to Siri's pace or expressiveness on compatible devices are synced to HomeView. HomeView features a wide variety of watchOS-style faces that can display snippets of information at a glance, a user's photos, or interactive art. With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView can integrate with compatible cameras to recognize people, pets, packages, and vehicles, and can describe captured video using AI. With Sound Recognition, HomeView can alert users to smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on their iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch. Similar to the security and privacy features of other Apple products, data processed by the A18 chip's Secure Exclaves is isolated from the HomeView software and does not leave the device. Users' personal content, like messages and calendar, is only displayed when the user's face is recognized and their iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked. The wall-mounted HomeView model can optionally be professionally installed. HomeView is made with 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure base and in the enclosure of the wall-mounted model, 100 percent gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today for US $299, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, November 13. The table-top model is available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray finishes, with the wall-mounted model available in space gray and silver finishes. Apple TV 4K With the A19 chip, Apple claims the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2X faster GPU performance when compared to the previous generation. In addition, a new, dedicated AV1 decoder enables more efficient streaming while using less bandwidth. Continuing on the theme of recent Apple product unveilings, the new Apple TV 4K supports Siri AI for smarter voice interactions. Users can find entertainment and control their smart home with more flexible natural language, and Siri AI's awareness of personal context and onscreen content can be used to answer questions about home events or what's currently playing. Users with an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad will be able to use Siri AI on Apple TV 4K (2nd and 3rd generation). Three far-field microphones on the new Apple TV 4K support Siri hands-free, allowing users to prompt it by saying "Siri" or "Hey Siri," as they do on other Apple devices. The new Siri Remote supports Find My with Precision Finding, which can guide users to the remote's precise location, useful if it, for example, falls between couch cushions. Like other Find My-capable devices, the remote can also play a sound to help users locate it. Similar to other Apple products, data processed by the Secure Exclaves is isolated from tvOS and does not leave the device. The new Apple TV 4K features 100 percent recycled gold plating and tin solder in all Apple-designed circuit boards, and 100 percent recycled rare earth elements in all magnets. It can be pre-ordered from Apple starting today for US $299, and will begin shipping to customers on Friday, November 13. Home Collection In collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, Apple has launched a collection of smart home accessories, including a lock, doorbell, thermostats, temperature sensors, and indoor and outdoor cameras. These accessories support NFC for one-tap setup on iPhone, and will begin rolling out in December.
en.body: Apple today announced updated models of the HomePod Mini and Apple TV 4K ; as well as an all-new HomeView smart home hub and a collection of smart home accessories .

en.title: Tindrift: Merge Roguelike
en.summary: One slide moves your whole army. Tindrift is a tactics roguelike built on slide-merge combat: same-class, same-rank soldiers merge into a higher rank, and every shadow acts by rule — no dice, ever. 100 floors across five acts, plus an Endless Drift, a Daily Seed and 1v1 duels. The campaign plays offline. NO LUCK TO BLAME Shadows telegraph the move they are about to make, gates cycle on a visible clock, and pits sit where you can plan around them. When a run ends you can name the exact slide that ended it — and when you win, you out-thought the board. YOU COMMAND AN ARMY, NOT A HERO Six soldier classes — vanguard, tank, medic, marksman, poisoner, support — merge only with their own kind, so every squad trades coverage against raw power. Set the formation before you climb: tank into the crowd, marksman down the long lane, medic in the middle. es.title: Orbit Strata 40: la nueva línea Braille de 40 celdas que llegará al mercado en octubre
es.summary: Orbit Research prepara el lanzamiento de una nueva línea Braille portátil con 40 celdas, teclado Perkins y conexión Bluetooth. El dispositivo también permite leer libros y tomar notas sin depender de un ordenador. La tiflotecnología sigue avanzando con nuevas alternativas para acceder a la información mediante el tacto. Una de las novedades previstas para este […] La entrada Orbit Strata 40: la nueva línea Braille de 40 celdas que llegará al mercado en octubre se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Orbit Research prepara el lanzamiento de una nueva línea Braille portátil con 40 celdas, teclado Perkins y conexión Bluetooth. El dispositivo también permite leer libros y tomar notas sin depender de un ordenador.

La tiflotecnología sigue avanzando con nuevas alternativas para acceder a la información mediante el tacto. Una de las novedades previstas para este otoño es el Orbit Strata 40 , una línea Braille diseñada para combinar lectura, escritura y conectividad en un único dispositivo.

La compañía Orbit Research presentó esta familia de productos en marzo de 2026, durante la conferencia CSUN Assistive Technology Conference. Su objetivo es ampliar las opciones disponibles para las personas ciegas que utilizan dispositivos Braille en sus estudios, su trabajo o su vida cotidiana.

No consta que esté disponible para su compra directa .

La página oficial de Orbit Research anuncia que el Strata 40 estará a la venta en octubre de 2026. Sin embargo, a fecha de 10 de octubre, la web sigue ofreciendo un formulario para apuntarse a una lista de espera y recibir un aviso cuando comiencen los envíos.

Por tanto, aunque el lanzamiento está previsto para este mes, no podemos confirmar que ya se esté comercializando ni que se pueda adquirir desde España. La empresa dispone de una red internacional de distribuidores, entre ellos ONCE-CIDAT, pero será necesario consultarles para conocer la disponibilidad y el precio en España.

El precio anunciado por el fabricante es de 2.595 dólares . Esta cifra no debe interpretarse como un precio final en euros, ya que pueden variar los impuestos, los gastos de distribución y las condiciones de venta.

El Orbit Strata 40 incorpora 40 celdas Braille actualizables de ocho puntos , que permiten leer información digital mediante el tacto. A diferencia de los modelos tradicionales de la familia Orbit Reader, este dispositivo utiliza tecnología piezoeléctrica.

El equipo integra un teclado Braille de ocho teclas, con distribución tipo Perkins, y controles de navegación para desplazarse por documentos y menús. También dispone de teclas de posicionamiento del cursor, que permiten situarse directamente en un punto concreto del texto.

Su diseño compacto busca facilitar el transporte y el uso diario. Según las especificaciones oficiales, pesa aproximadamente 600 gramos y mide 30 × 9,5 × 2,8 centímetros.

Una de las características más interesantes del Strata 40 es que puede utilizarse de forma independiente o conectado a un ordenador o teléfono móvil.

En modo autónomo, permite leer libros y documentos, tomar notas y editar archivos. También incorpora herramientas como calendario, reloj, alarma y calculadora.

El dispositivo admite archivos de texto y formatos Braille como BRF y BRL. Además, integra traducción Braille en ambos sentidos para más de 70 idiomas, según el fabricante.

Estas funciones pueden resultar útiles para estudiantes, profesionales y usuarios que quieran consultar documentos o escribir notas sin tener que recurrir constantemente a otro equipo.

El Orbit Strata 40 también funciona como línea Braille externa. Puede conectarse mediante USB-C o Bluetooth a ordenadores y dispositivos móviles compatibles.

Orbit Research indica que es compatible con lectores de pantalla habituales en Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, ChromeOS, Fire OS y Linux. Además, permite mantener conectados hasta cinco dispositivos y cambiar entre ellos.

Esta posibilidad puede facilitar el trabajo de quienes alternan entre el ordenador, el teléfono móvil y otros equipos durante la jornada.

El fabricante también destaca su batería de larga duración, la carga rápida y la resistencia al polvo y a los líquidos. Incluye una ranura para tarjetas SD y permite acceder a archivos almacenados en memorias USB.

La principal diferencia está en la combinación de una línea de 40 celdas, funciones de anotador y tecnología piezoeléctrica en un formato portátil.

La nueva familia Strata también incluye otros modelos. El Strata 40 Pro añade funciones multimedia, síntesis de voz, conectividad Wi-Fi y aplicaciones integradas más amplias. Por su parte, el Strata 20 Pro ofrece un formato de 20 celdas con funciones multimodales.

Conviene no confundirlos: el Strata 40 estándar está pensado para leer, escribir y conectarse con otros equipos, mientras que las versiones Pro amplían las posibilidades con voz, audio y servicios adicionales.

El Orbit Strata 40 es una de las novedades relevantes de la tiflotecnología anunciadas para 2026. Su combinación de lectura Braille, anotación y conectividad puede resultar interesante para quienes buscan un dispositivo portátil para estudiar, trabajar o acceder a documentos digitales.

No obstante, todavía quedan cuestiones prácticas por confirmar para los usuarios en España: la fecha efectiva de los primeros envíos, la disponibilidad a través de distribuidores nacionales y el precio final en euros.

Desde el punto de vista de la accesibilidad, el lanzamiento amplía las alternativas existentes para acceder a la información mediante Braille. Habrá que esperar a conocer su disponibilidad comercial y las condiciones de distribución para valorar su llegada al mercado español.

Estado del producto: lanzamiento anunciado para octubre de 2026; la web oficial sigue indicando que hay que apuntarse a la lista de espera para recibir un aviso cuando comiencen los envíos.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes consultadas: Página oficial del Strata 40 , distribuidoras internacionales , SightCity .

en.body:
Published 9 October 2026 by Quin

Paperback is a fast, fully accessible reader for ebooks, documents and audio books. It opens over twenty formats and speaks sixteen languages.

Opening documents:

Reading and listening:

Paperback has two ways to read a document. In text mode, you read the text with your screen reader. In read aloud mode, Paperback reads the text to you with the voice you pick in Settings, and keeps going in the background and from the lock screen. Switch between them from the More Options menu. Audio books, like DAISY, M4B, and MP3 books, play their own recording instead.

The reading bar:

The bar at the bottom of the screen has, from left to right:

You can also swipe up or down on the play button to move by the navigation unit, without reaching for the previous and next buttons. If that is all you use, the Hide previous and next buttons setting takes them out of your screen reader’s way. The Swipe up moves forward setting picks which way a swipe goes.

More options

The More Options menu is where everything else lives.

Keyboards and headsets:

With a keyboard, the desktop shortcuts for opening books, recent documents, Find, Go To, the table of contents, word count, document info, export, and the sleep timer all work. So do the single-letter keys for moving by heading, page, link, and the rest, and Space plays and pauses. A headset button plays and pauses with one press, moves forward with two, and goes back with three.

Paperback was designed with screen readers, and works flawlessly with both TalkBack and Backtalk.

en.title: Getting Started: Essential ZoomText and Fusion Features for the Workplace
en.summary: ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech. Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful …
en.body:
ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech.

Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful features of ZoomText and Fusion that will help you be more productive in the workplace. This blog series will run throughout October, with a new post every Thursday featuring helpful information and practical tips to make the most of ZoomText and Fusion as you work. To help you get started, we’ll highlight some of the most important ZoomText and Fusion features that can make your daily work tasks easier and more efficient.

ZoomText and Fusion offer flexible magnification , letting you choose the level that works best for your tasks and environment. You can select from different zoom window types —like full screen, lens, or docked—and even use multiple monitors for expanded workspace. Advanced Smoothing, including xFont and Geometric Smoothing, keeps text and graphics sharp and easy to read at any magnification level.

Color Enhancements allow you to adjust color settings for better clarity. You can apply preset color schemes, switch to two-color modes, or replace specific problem colors to make on-screen content easier to see. These options help reduce eye strain, especially during long workdays.

Focus enhancements help you track your position in menus, dialogs, and application controls, so you never lose your place. Mouse pointers and cursors can be customized in size and color, making them easier to spot and follow on the screen.

AppReader is a built-in tool that reads documents, web pages, and emails aloud, supporting users who need to hear text read aloud. This is extremely useful for users who experience eye fatigue when reading long documents and emails.

For Fusion users, the full JAWS screen reader is included, adding speech and Braille support to all ZoomText magnification features. JAWS features like Say All (which reads from your cursor position), virtual cursor navigation for web pages and applications, and Quick Navigation keys for navigating web pages make workplace tasks more accessible. Fusion lets you switch seamlessly between magnification and speech, depending on your needs.

With ZoomText and Fusion, you can customize your environment to match your vision needs and adjust settings at any time as your tasks change. You can also save your personalized settings, so your preferred setup is always ready whenever you start your work day.

Stay tuned for Week 2, where we’ll explore how to use ZoomText and Fusion across your workday, from Microsoft Word to Teams, to help you stay productive and connected. We’ll discuss important ZoomText and Fusion settings, plus provide tips for navigating workplace apps with more confidence and ease.

Have questions? Email training@vispero.com .

en.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Review: I Keep Coming Back to the Pro
en.summary: The last couple years have been big for iPhone. In 2025, Apple introduced two brand new iPhone models: iPhone 16e, an entry-level model with most of the essential components of the more expensive iPhones of its generation; and iPhone Air, the thinnest-ever iPhone to date at the time. This year, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, the company's first-ever foldable iPhone and with it, a whole new form factor and way of using iPhone as we know it. In between the new iPhone models, Apple has, year-by-year, continued the steady evolution of its Pro and Pro Max phones. This year, for the first time, I had the opportunity to review both iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. One of the devices was a review unit on loan from Apple, whilst the other was the phone I purchased for myself. Being able to use both devices, one after the other, gave me a unique opportunity to evaluate them side-by-side, and I have a much deeper appreciation for each model and its strengths (and limitations). And after spending time with each phone, I came away with a surprising and yet inevitable conclusion: while iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are similar, they are very different devices for very different use cases. And only one of them is a device I would routinely recommend for most people. Getting a Feel for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max On the surface, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are almost identical to last year's devices. Cosmic Orange is out in favor of Burgundy and Glacier [light blue], but on the outside at least, not much else has changed. iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max come in Black, Silver, Glacier [light blue], and Burgundy. Both devices have a Super Retina XDR display with Ceramic Shield 2; forged unibody featuring an Apple-designed 7000 series aluminum alloy; and a color-matched glass back with Ceramic Shield. iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the display on iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. (Displays are measured diagonally.) The left edge of the device houses the Volume Buttons. The right edge of the device has the Side Button at the top and the Camera Control towards the bottom. The bottom edge of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max holds the bottom speaker on the left, a USB-C port in the middle, and the microphone on the right. There are three different cameras on the top back of the device, housed in the plateau. The plateau extends across approximately the top third of the back of the device. The back glass feels very similar in texture to the forged unibody. In my hand—that all-important ‘hand-feel’—iPhone 18 Pro feels, as Goldilocks would say, ‘just right’. It is appropriately heavy—‘substantial’—and is neither so big such that holding it one-handed is likely to be difficult for most; nor is it so small that one must compromise on battery life or overall form and function. Whereas iPhone 18 Pro feels ideal for most, iPhone 18 Pro Max is absolutely huge in comparison and almost feels unwieldy. It is heavy in the hand and even heavier in the pocket of my khakis. One-handed usage is not really an option, though if you are already used to and comfortable with the Pro Max phones, do note that iPhone 18 Pro Max has not changed in size. Battery Life iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback with up to 24 hours of typical usage per charge, while iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours of video playback and up to 30 hours of typical usage per charge. In my experience, battery life on even the smaller iPhone 18 Pro has been enough to get me through the day, and then some. On a typical day, I finished with around 40% battery remaining on iPhone 18 Pro and 60% on iPhone 18 Pro Max, give or take. The lowest I got the iPhone 18 Pro was 21% on my very first full day with the device, and the lowest I got the 18 Pro Max was 32% on a day when, unbeknownst to me, screen brightness got set to 100% and Screen Curtain became disabled. Not counting the days when the erroneous settings were a factor, my next-lowest end-of-day battery reading on iPhone 18 Pro Max was 46% after a little over 18 hours off the charger. On one day with exceptionally light usage, I finished at 64% with iPhone 18 Pro and 81% with iPhone 18 Pro Max. Performance iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max both share Apple’s latest and greatest A20 Pro processor and an improved cooling system. While I do not use my phones for processor-intensive work, what I can say is that day-to-day performance of the A20 Pro is as good as you could possibly want it to be. Apps and screens open quickly, and the operating system runs well. VoiceOver—Apple’s built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users—responds as soon as I touch the screen. There is no latency whatsoever. When compared to last year’s A19 Pro, in day-to-day device usage, I noticed hardly any difference with this year's A20 Pro in iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The A19 series of processors already ran iOS 27 and VoiceOver exceptionally well, with Apple definitely appearing to have done some serious work to make VoiceOver feel more snappy. Usually, when one installs a new major update, there is a small decrease in VoiceOver responsiveness; this was not the case for me this year running iOS 27 on iPhone 17 Pro Max. (I also tested several of the iOS 27 betas on an iPhone 17e with the regular A19 processor, and my experience was the same.) Given that performance of the A19 Pro was already incredibly good in everyday usage, it should come as no surprise then that this year’s A20 Pro is only nominally better for the same types of work. It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try. In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app. Speakers and Sound When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to. iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed. It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker. Siri AI While not specifically a new feature of this year's iPhones, Siri got a major upgrade in iOS 27. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful. And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case. Camera, Cellular, and Other Things One of the headline new features of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is the 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. Being blind, I am not able to speak firsthand to this and, while I had a very interesting discussion with ChatGPT on variable aperture and what this might mean in practical terms, I am not comfortable including any of that here as I cannot independently verify its accuracy. For an in-depth evaluation of the iPhone 18 Pro camera specifically, I recommend this review by PetaPixel's Jaron Schneider. iPhone 18 Pro (specifically) has the Apple C2 modem, and both models have the Apple N1 wireless networking chip. In my speed tests, the only meaningful difference between the C2 modem in iPhone 18 Pro and the modem in iPhone 18 Pro Max was that the C2 on iPhone 18 Pro seemed to deliver upload speeds that were slightly faster. Testing was done on the T-Mobile network in Chicago. As spotted by AppleVis user Zach M, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max support 8-dot braille in Braille Screen Input (BSI), and calibration of braille dots in BSI now works similar to how it is on iPad. Not being familiar with 8-dot braille, I cannot speak to this firsthand. Due to the size of its battery, iPhone 18 Pro Max has a "Prepare to Ship" option that one must use to sufficiently discharge the battery and limit battery capacity prior to shipping it for repair or any other reason. This Apple Support Article has more info. With a compatible adapter, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max can charge up to 50% in 15 minutes. While I do not think I have the prerequisite adapter for this, my own subjective experience is that charging is faster than on last year's model. Which Phone Should I Buy? As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions. Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space. With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term. Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand. If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use. When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors. The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely. Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market. Conclusion On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

The last couple years have been big for iPhone.

In 2025, Apple introduced two brand new iPhone models: iPhone 16e, an entry-level model with most of the essential components of the more expensive iPhones of its generation; and iPhone Air, the thinnest-ever iPhone to date at the time. This year, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, the company's first-ever foldable iPhone and with it, a whole new form factor and way of using iPhone as we know it.

In between the new iPhone models, Apple has, year-by-year, continued the steady evolution of its Pro and Pro Max phones. This year, for the first time, I had the opportunity to review both iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. One of the devices was a review unit on loan from Apple, whilst the other was the phone I purchased for myself. Being able to use both devices, one after the other, gave me a unique opportunity to evaluate them side-by-side, and I have a much deeper appreciation for each model and its strengths (and limitations). And after spending time with each phone, I came away with a surprising and yet inevitable conclusion: while iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are similar, they are very different devices for very different use cases. And only one of them is a device I would routinely recommend for most people.

On the surface, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are almost identical to last year's devices. Cosmic Orange is out in favor of Burgundy and Glacier [light blue], but on the outside at least, not much else has changed.

iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max come in Black, Silver, Glacier [light blue], and Burgundy. Both devices have a Super Retina XDR display with Ceramic Shield 2; forged unibody featuring an Apple-designed 7000 series aluminum alloy; and a color-matched glass back with Ceramic Shield. iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the display on iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. (Displays are measured diagonally.) The left edge of the device houses the Volume Buttons. The right edge of the device has the Side Button at the top and the Camera Control towards the bottom. The bottom edge of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max holds the bottom speaker on the left, a USB-C port in the middle, and the microphone on the right.

There are three different cameras on the top back of the device, housed in the plateau. The plateau extends across approximately the top third of the back of the device. The back glass feels very similar in texture to the forged unibody.

In my hand—that all-important ‘hand-feel’—iPhone 18 Pro feels, as Goldilocks would say, ‘just right’. It is appropriately heavy—‘substantial’—and is neither so big such that holding it one-handed is likely to be difficult for most; nor is it so small that one must compromise on battery life or overall form and function.

Whereas iPhone 18 Pro feels ideal for most, iPhone 18 Pro Max is absolutely huge in comparison and almost feels unwieldy. It is heavy in the hand and even heavier in the pocket of my khakis. One-handed usage is not really an option, though if you are already used to and comfortable with the Pro Max phones, do note that iPhone 18 Pro Max has not changed in size.

iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback with up to 24 hours of typical usage per charge, while iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours of video playback and up to 30 hours of typical usage per charge. In my experience, battery life on even the smaller iPhone 18 Pro has been enough to get me through the day, and then some.

On a typical day, I finished with around 40% battery remaining on iPhone 18 Pro and 60% on iPhone 18 Pro Max, give or take. The lowest I got the iPhone 18 Pro was 21% on my very first full day with the device, and the lowest I got the 18 Pro Max was 32% on a day when, unbeknownst to me, screen brightness got set to 100% and Screen Curtain became disabled. Not counting the days when the erroneous settings were a factor, my next-lowest end-of-day battery reading on iPhone 18 Pro Max was 46% after a little over 18 hours off the charger. On one day with exceptionally light usage, I finished at 64% with iPhone 18 Pro and 81% with iPhone 18 Pro Max.

iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max both share Apple’s latest and greatest A20 Pro processor and an improved cooling system. While I do not use my phones for processor-intensive work, what I can say is that day-to-day performance of the A20 Pro is as good as you could possibly want it to be. Apps and screens open quickly, and the operating system runs well. VoiceOver—Apple’s built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users—responds as soon as I touch the screen. There is no latency whatsoever.

When compared to last year’s A19 Pro, in day-to-day device usage, I noticed hardly any difference with this year's A20 Pro in iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The A19 series of processors already ran iOS 27 and VoiceOver exceptionally well, with Apple definitely appearing to have done some serious work to make VoiceOver feel more snappy. Usually, when one installs a new major update, there is a small decrease in VoiceOver responsiveness; this was not the case for me this year running iOS 27 on iPhone 17 Pro Max. (I also tested several of the iOS 27 betas on an iPhone 17e with the regular A19 processor, and my experience was the same.) Given that performance of the A19 Pro was already incredibly good in everyday usage, it should come as no surprise then that this year’s A20 Pro is only nominally better for the same types of work. It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try.

In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app.

When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to.

iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed.

It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker.

While not specifically a new feature of this year's iPhones, Siri got a major upgrade in iOS 27. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful.

And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case.

As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions.

Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space.

With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term.

Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand.

If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use.

When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying.
