en.title: In-Process 28th September 2026
en.summary: Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3! NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 Changes to the Changes Our International Communities Copying last spoken text Talking about NVDA Show Screen Overview NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3. Firstly, do go back and read all… Read More
en.body:
Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3!

As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3 . Firstly, do go back and read all about NVDA 2026.2 if needed, but otherwise, let’s dive into what is coming up in NVDA 2026.3:

This release includes significant performance improvements, improvements to NVDA’s dialogs, and expanded touch screen input.

Several performance improvements have been made to reduce lag and improve responsiveness. NVDA now fetches and caches more information about controls in the background, improving performance in controls such as combo boxes and File Explorer. NVDA no longer causes File Explorer or other applications to crash when NVDA is exited or restarted. NVDA now recovers more quickly when an application stops responding, and will no longer freeze or flood the log with errors from unresponsive applications. In live text regions, such as terminals, NVDA no longer freezes when substantial amounts of text are dumped to the screen.

Context menus and keyboard shortcuts have been added to the Configuration Profiles, Input Gestures, and Speech Dictionaries dialogs, making these dialogs easier to use with the keyboard. It is also now possible to change an existing gesture directly in the Input Gestures dialog. The dialog used to present browsable messages has been modernized and now better supports resizing, maximizing, and minimizing.

Touch screen input has been significantly expanded. Sequential two-flick gestures now combine two flicks in quick succession into a single gesture, greatly increasing the number of bindable touch gestures. Edge gestures are also now supported, allowing gestures that begin within 15 mm of any screen edge to be bound independently from the same gesture performed in the centre of the screen.

A new unassigned command has been added to move the mouse cursor to the centre of the magnified view. Windows OCR can now be used while the Screen Curtain or NVDA’s built-in Magnifier is active.

Liblouis has been updated with new Elfdalian, Sami, Maori, New Zealand Unified English Braille, and Haitian Creole braille tables, a Norwegian table for Spanish text, and additional Swedish 6 and 8 dot variants. eSpeak NG has been updated with added support for Ligurian and Abkhaz.

Updates to translations Fix bug with Magnifier’s “Show screen overview” feature when using relative tracking mode Updated eSpeak In browse mode, alt+upArrow and alt+downArrow now collapse or expand combo boxes in more situations Prevent flashing from shifting magnifier colour filters to reduce seizure risk Update to the Chinese Word Segmentation library cppjieba to fix startup crashes from Chinese paths

If you’ve looked at the changes document for the NVDA 2026.3 betas , you might have noticed a change to the formatting. Or rather, some new formatting. Instead of having a list of features, and then breaking that up into sub-lists of Braille features and Touch Screen features and Browse mode features, we’ve made them headings:

“What’s new in NVDA” is at the top of the document and is a heading level 1 – press shift+1 to jump back to that from anywhere (or control+home since it’s at the top of the document). The version of NVDA, “2026.3”, “2026.2” etc, is a heading level 2. Press 2 to jump to the next older version of NVDA, or shift+2 to jump back to the start of the current version, or next newest version of NVDA. “New features”, “Changes”, “Bug Fixes”, “Changes for Developers”, “Security fixes”, and “Important notes” are all Heading level 3. sub-headings in the section, new features, changes, etc, are heading level 4. In the “New Features” for NVDA 2026.3 for instance, press 4 to jump to “Braille”, “Touch Screen Input”, “Browse Mode”, which are all sections of new features for this version.

If you are used to simply arrowing down through the list and reading each feature, that still works as it did. Or if you press i to jump between list items, that will still work, although you will miss the heading. If you navigate like that and hear “List with x items” and you’re not sure what the list is, press shift+h to jump to the previous heading (at any level) and it will move to the heading just before the list. As something new, we’re interested in what you think – good or bad. It’s the first time we’ve changed the formatting in awhile (though not the first at all, though the last change will not have been as noticeable to all our users).

While we’ve been sprucing things up, we recently gave the “ Connect with the NVDA Community ” page a once over. Firstly, we made sure all the links worked and followed up those with problems. As a result of that, we’ve removed a couple in consultation with their owners (Finnish and Swedish particularly) and added a couple more we had found along the way (Hi to our friends from the Brazilian Portuguese site!)

We also took the opportunity to add headings at H3 for each language, so you can jump or link to the Romanian resources directly now.

We’re always interested in adding new resources to the list. Are you aware of any other groups we’re not aware of? Particularly in languages not yet listed there. Please get in touch if you know of any.

One of the popular features in NVDA 2026.2 was the addition of NVDA+x to repeat the last spoken information. You could press that twice quickly to have the information displayed in a dialog so you could read it with more granular control. If what you want to do is copy the information, while you can do it from that dialog, we’ve added a new command to NVDA 2026.3 to make it even easier. Press NVDA+control+x to copy the last spoken information directly to the clipboard. Thank you to community contributor Cary for his work on this feature!

(A screenshot of the original NVDA+x double press dialog, showing the new feature bullet point for the NVDA+control+x command. Note the dialog has white text on black, because I had the magnifier running with colours inverted when I took the screenshot.)

We love talking about NVDA! I often forget to mention interviews here, but we’ve recently done a couple I thought I’d share:

Access Point Firstly, our “Access Point” collaboration with World Services for the Blind continues with the second in our podcast series, on everything new in NVDA 2026.2.

Tek Talk Next, Training & Support Manager Quentin was on Tek Talk , again covering everything new with NVDA.

And, on a slightly different topic NOT involving us talking – but if YOU love talking about NVDA, accessibility and navigation, Monash University, in Australia, are offering a paid PhD Scholarship in Communication and Navigation for Blind and Low Vision People .

Monash are looking for a linguist or researcher with a related background to investigate how Blind and Low Vision people navigate the world using technology.

The project focuses on video ethnography, multimodal communication, and users’ experiences of navigation technology, with opportunities to collaborate with researchers in assistive technology and AI.

This is open to both Australians and International applicants It’s also part of the Monash Assistive Technology and Society Centre (MATS) and Monash AI Institute so the successful applicant will have lots of opportunity to collaborate with technologists about building better navigational tech going forward.

Do refer to the position description at Monash for all the details.

One of the features of the magnifier we didn’t mention much last time is the Show Entire Screen Overview. Since one of the fixes in the latest NVDA 2026.3 beta is a fix involving this feature, I thought it was worth a mention. So firstly, the fix is that it WILL now work if using relative tracking mode – so if you prefer that magnifier tracking mode, you might want to upgrade before trying it out.

With the magnifier running, press NVDA+shift+L to “Show entire screen”. This temporarily zooms out to show the whole screen (as if the magnifier wasn’t running). After a couple of seconds without the mouse moving, the view zooms back in again.

Because the view smoothly zooms out and then back in again, it makes it easier to tell where the zoomed area is in relation to the whole screen. By waiting for mouse movement to stop, it allows a user to explore the unmagnified view and then smoothly zooms in to where the focus currently is.

If you wish to instantly enable or disable the magnifier, NVDA+shift+w will do this immediately, without zoom out (and then only magnifies again once you press NVDA+shift+w again).

Another difference is that pressing NVDA+shift+L zooms out but leaves any colour filtering enabled. If you wish to quickly zoom out and remove colour filtering, then you may find turning off the magnifier ( NVDA+shift+w ) works better.

And a related tip – if you don’t want magnification BUT do want colour filtering, you can enable the magnifier, enable colour filtering ( NVDA+shift+i ) and then zoom out to 1x ( NVDA+shift+minus ).

That’s all for this week. A little longer than it sometimes is, but there we covered quite a few keystrokes – did you learn any new ones? Surely at least NVDA+control+x ? Do try out the latest 2026.3 beta, and some of those commands. Do please keep giving feedback on the changes and improvements. Also please do share any other international communities we aren’t yet aware of.

en.title: LiveComics
en.summary: LiveComics is a comic, manga, and manhwa reader that performs the page as audio rather than simply displaying it. Every speech bubble is voiced in…
en.body:
Published 25 September 2026 by Matt T

LiveComics is a comic, manga, and manhwa reader that performs the page as audio rather than simply displaying it. Every speech bubble is voiced in character, with a separate narrator, while each panel can include its own sound effects and score. The reader advances panel by panel as the scene plays, allowing a whole issue to be followed without seeing the screen.

The app streams a free shelf of classic public-domain issues. Readers can also import their own CBR and CBZ files on the web and read them on the phone.

A free account covers the core service with no card required. A paid storage tier is available through the website, with no in-app purchases.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Tested with TalkBack. A comic is a purely visual medium, and this app performs the whole issue as audio: every line is voiced in character with a separate narrator, the drawn sound effects actually sound, and a score runs under the scene, so a complete story can be followed with the screen off. On navigation, the library, the store, the menus and the reader controls all work without a mouse and report themselves to the screen reader, and cover tiles are real buttons rather than tappable images. Turning a panel announces your position and nothing else, for example "page 3, panel 5 of 40", and that silence is deliberate so the screen reader does not talk over the narration. The panel's own words are available separately, in a hidden region named "Panel text" holding the description, the dialogue line by line and the drawn sound lettering; nothing in it is ever announced on its own, so a braille display can read it without fighting the audio. Dialogs take focus when they open and hand it back when they close, Escape closes them, screen changes are announced politely because the app never reloads the page, and segmented controls report which option is selected. Automated checks are clean, with axe reporting 0 serious or critical issues, though that is a floor rather than a claim about real use. For low vision, the reader crops to a single panel, fills the screen with it and then advances on its own as the scene plays, which is magnification you do not have to drive, with no pinching and no hunting for the next balloon. Known issues and limitations, stated plainly: the "Panel text" region is easy to miss, because it never announces itself and nothing in the reader tells you it is there; Tab is not trapped inside dialogs; the library's medium filter (All, Comics, Manga, Manhwa) does not report which option is currently selected; there is no audio-first onboarding, so signing up and importing a file still assume you can work an ordinary form; the collision between the screen reader and the narration has never been deliberately tested across a range of devices, so we cannot promise the ducking behaves the same everywhere; and NVDA on Windows and iOS VoiceOver have never been run at all, so with the phone app loading the same code as the website, Windows behaviour in particular is unverified.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7, Android 16

en.title: Google Is Rolling Out Guided Vision to Gemini Live: Here’s How to Use It and My Early Impressions
en.summary: Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in…
en.body:
Published 23 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Google allows users to turn on the camera feed while in a conversation with Gemini Live, so they can ask about things that are in view. Although a blind user can take advantage of this feature, it is not designed specifically to assist blind people. Google is now rolling out Guided vision, a mode that uses the camera in a live conversation to help blind people get an overview of their surroundings, read text, and more. This post covers turning the feature on and using it, as well as my first impressions from testing it.

Note that I haven’t done anything special to access Guided vision on my Honor 600 Pro, but I am running a three-month AI Pro trial that came as an offer with my device, so I don’t know if that affected the feature’s arrival on my device. The feature is not available for my other Accessible Android colleagues yet.

Table of Contents

To enable Guided vision:

A notification appears on the screen with the ability to start a Live session directly. When you use the button to start the Live session, it starts with the camera feed enabled, so you can start talking.

Note that the feature is still not available for everyone, so you should wait if you cannot find the Guided vision toggle in Settings.

According to the Google Accessibility help article , it’s possible to assign Guided vision to an accessibility shortcut, and you can launch it through TalkBack too. However, both are still not available on my device. In fact, I haven’t received any TalkBack update recently.

I haven’t tested to see if launching the camera in a Live conversation when Guided vision is active uses the mode without any user’s intervention, but during my tests, I always asked Gemini to start Guided vision to make sure that it works in that mode. When I tried to prompt the assistant to start the feature, it asked me to point the camera at what I wanted described, but that was one of its hallucinations, as it didn’t open the camera feed or start the Live conversation. Starting a Live conversation is still necessary.

At another time, I asked it to start a Live conversation with Guided vision, but at that instance, it told me that it couldn’t start it automatically and asked me to start Live manually.

Note that turning off Guided vision and then turning it back on from Settings shows the notification to start a Live conversation again, which can be used to start a conversation with the camera turned on.

When I had my first conversation with Live with Guided vision turned on, Gemini reminded me that it cannot detect all hazards or guarantee path clearance and that I should use my mobility aid before almost every response. I kept telling it that I understand the risks and that it shouldn’t repeat those warnings. During the later conversations, I didn’t hear any of the warnings. I am not sure, though, if my early prompting helped, or if you hear those warnings only during the first conversation to alert you of the risks or when Gemini thinks that it should do so for your safety.

During conversations with Guided vision active, I couldn’t find any indication that a special mode is active. All Live-related controls are the same, with no difference. However, the difference is in how Gemini acts. During my short tests, I found that Gemini tried to be detailed in its descriptions because it was aware that Guided vision is active and that the mode is designed to assist blind users.

I was able to ask it questions about the mode, and I got assurance from it that the mode is to assist blind users. It gave me guidance on how to move the camera to show certain objects or scenes better. When I asked it to tell me how to move to reach something, it told me that it needed to know exactly where I was in relation to the camera’s orientation. Using my hand as a reference, it gave me directions with respect to my hand. It also described the positions of items in the room relative to each other, like the position of a fan relative to the sofa.

Additionally, Gemini told me the book that I was holding and tried to assist me in putting the full page in view. When I asked it to read the page, it read a part of the page, though. However, when I asked it if that was the only text on the page, it correctly stated that there were other texts and visual diagrams and offered to describe them for me.

These observations are based on my initial tests, and I haven’t made direct comparisons between using Guided vision with the feature turned on and using the normal Live camera mode with it turned off.

Guided vision changes only how Gemini tries to provide information, as well as making it give more hints to assist a blind user. However, it is still a part of the Live experience. This means that current Live limitations are still present. The most important limitation is the need to prompt it again to tell you about any change, as Live doesn’t have real-time monitoring or continuous picture analysis capabilities.

Another factor worth mentioning is the model used, as Guided vision doesn’t switch Gemini to a more capable AI model than the one that you are using in your Gemini app.

Although image analysis has already advanced and helps in many scenarios, misidentifications are always a part of the formula that shouldn’t be forgotten. For example, a towel hanging on a door was identified more than once as pink, although it wasn’t pink.

Additionally, leveraging the new mode to take pictures still needs work. After Gemini gave me directions to centre my face and I told it to take a photo, it obeyed my order, opened the camera, and took a photo, but that led to the termination of the Live session. That behavior ended the conversation without being able to make sure that the photo was properly captured or without asking any additional questions about what it includes.

Guided vision is an interesting step forward from Google in tailoring Live camera to blind users. Although Google still has the Lookout app , it decided to make Guided vision a part of the Gemini app. Google decided to launch the feature and mention TalkBack as one of the methods to turn it on before releasing a TalkBack update that includes the necessary shortcut. There is even no accessibility service that can be assigned to an accessibility shortcut at the time of writing. However, an interesting thing for users who rely on other screen readers is that using the feature is not tied to having TalkBack running. I am almost sure that Gemini doesn’t check whether a screen reader is running as a requirement to use the feature.

Although it is in its early stages, I am excited to keep Guided vision on, and I am not considering going back to the normal camera mode. This should minimize the need to remind Gemini that I am blind or to try to speak prompts asking it to help me guide my camera toward the subject I am asking about or the text I want it to help me read.

Google doesn’t lack the resources to improve how Guided vision works, with the money and ability to make Gemini Live a trusted assistant, as much as “trusted” can be used with AI services, that understands the needs of blind people and helps them live a more independent life.

Published in Reviews Tutorials

en.summary: Accessimind Reader is a screen reader application developed to enable visually impaired and partially sighted users to use their Android phones more clearly, quickly, and…
en.body:
Published 19 September 2026 by Sarper Arıkan

Accessimind Reader is a screen reader application developed to enable visually impaired and partially sighted users to use their Android phones more clearly, quickly, and independently.

Accessimind Reader uses the Android AccessibilityService API to provide screen reading functions. AccessibilityService is used to provide audio versions of on-screen content, detect user interface elements, navigate with gestures, provide audio feedback on focused items, and deliver a screen reader experience. This service is necessary for the screen reading feature, which is the core function of the application, to work.

Accessimind Reader does not use AccessibilityService for user tracking, displaying advertisements, remotely recording calls, bypassing Android security mechanisms, or modifying user settings without permission.

The application presents audio feedback, gesture navigation, keyboard shortcuts, clipboard operations, reading preferences, and tools for the focused item in a practical accessibility flow. The context menu provides quick access to frequently used areas such as reading controls, clipboard operations, notification access, focused item operations, and Accessimind settings.

Key Features:

Accessimind Reader is designed for users who need voice output and fast navigation. It focuses on providing predictable controls, understandable labels, and quick access to frequently used screen reader operations.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Accessimind is a screen reader. Users can test it to see how well its features work for them and fit their needs.

en.title: iPhone 18 Pro: Hands-On and Initial Impressions
en.summary: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will be available to customers on Friday, September 18, 2026. Ahead of the launch, Apple sent me an iPhone 18 Pro for review. While a full review will come once I’ve had the opportunity to live with iPhone 18 Pro for a while, I do have some initial impressions that I wanted to share. First, and perhaps most noticeably, iPhone 18 Pro has what I would describe as a really big sound for its size. When compared side-by-side to iPhone 17 Pro Max—a device much larger and, presumably, with a bigger bottom speaker—iPhone 18 Pro sounds warmer, fuller, and lacks the treble over-emphasis I observed on the iPhone 17 Pro Max. If I had to describe the sound of iPhone 18 Pro, it would be ‘more complete’. And I do not think it is just software-side equalization: even at a relatively low 25% volume, iPhone 18 Pro has more bass and overall ‘presence’. My best guess is that Apple has made some hardware changes to the speaker on iPhone 18 Pro, and hopefully the iPhone 18 Pro Max too. One last note on sound for now: the earpiece speaker sounds warmer and fuller, as well. Beyond the speaker, iPhone 18 Pro contains some useful under-the-hood improvements, one of which I was not expecting to notice. Compared to last year’s models, iPhone 18 Pro has a larger vaper chamber inside the device for added cooling capacity. This is not just something you hear about at a Keynote and that's the end of it: picking up iPhone 18 Pro on multiple occasions, I noticed how literally 'cool' it felt to the touch. And even after multiple long phone calls on two different occasions, iPhone 18 Pro did not feel warm the way my iPhone 17 Pro Max does under similar circumstances. Cellular performance on iPhone 18 Pro's Apple-designed C2 Modem seems very good so far. On T-Mobile in Chicago, I got speeds right around a gigabyte down while indoors and a grand total of 1,109 Mbps down / 236 Mbps up when outdoors. This is not unheard-of for my area, but it is also not the norm, either. I will continue to test this throughout the review period. In terms of performance from the A20 Pro processor, VoiceOver (the built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision people) is as fast and responsive as one could possibly want it to be. The moment I put my finger on the screen, VoiceOver is off and talking. That said, VoiceOver in iOS 27 already runs exceptionally well on the A19 series of chips from last year’s devices, and there’s only so much “can this be any more responsive?” before you hit an inevitable ceiling. Is VoiceOver ‘more’ responsive on the A20 Pro processor in iPhone 18 Pro than last year’s A19 Pro? Yes, but not by much—and again, this is only because VoiceOver already runs so well on last year’s A19-equipped devices to begin with. And that’s about all I can confidently speak to right now. Battery life seems good so far, though of course it’s day one and any serious testing will need to wait until after the various background tasks finish in the next couple days. Performance is good. Sound is very good. Call quality and cellular performance also seem good. I am excited for the coming weeks. Watch this space.

en.title: Learn How to Work More Effectively with PDFs and JAWS
en.summary: PDF documents are everywhere, from reports and forms to manuals and online resources. These documents can be accessed via a web browser or application like Adobe Acrobat Reader. When PDFs are formatted correctly, they can be read using standard navigation commands and JAWS Quick Navigation Keys; however, challenges arise when the PDF is not structured …
en.body:
PDF documents are everywhere, from reports and forms to manuals and online resources. These documents can be accessed via a web browser or application like Adobe Acrobat Reader.

When PDFs are formatted correctly, they can be read using standard navigation commands and JAWS Quick Navigation Keys; however, challenges arise when the PDF is not structured correctly. Details like headings, reading order, table structure, and labeled form fields — tell JAWS what to say and in what order. Whether that structure exists at all, and whether it matches what a sighted reader sees, is what separates an accessible PDF from an inaccessible one.

Join us Thursday, September 17 at noon ET for a live webinar, “Beyond the Basics: Working More Effectively with PDF Documents and JAWS.” We’ll delve deeper into these challenges and provide tips for navigating PDFs more efficiently.

In this webinar, we’ll provide an overview of PDFs, plus show you how to:

Register for this webinar to improve proficiency and productivity when working with PDFs, and learn some troubleshooting tips along the way. ACVREP credits will be available for those who attend the live webinar.

Can’t attend? We archive all webinars on our Webinars on Demand page. Have questions? Send an email to training@vispero.com .

en.title: Jieshuo Touch Focus And Double Tap Delays
en.summary: Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the…
en.body:
Published 16 September 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Whether you are exploring the screen or trying to find a specific element, there is a delay between touching the screen and focusing on the element under your finger. Similar to TalkBack, Jieshuo screen reader allows you to change the value of this delay. It also allows you to set the time in which 2 taps are registered as an accessibility double tap.

In order to change the touch focus delay and double tap delay values, you must first enable handling gestures directly through Jieshuo. To do this, go to Advanced settings > Operation settings and check the Handle gestures in the screen reader checkbox.

The next item in this section is for setting the touch focus delay value. Available values are 150, 200, 250, and 300 milliseconds. To change the time for double tap registration, select Double tap delay and choose any of the available values. The same values as those available for the touch focus delay are provided here.

In the same settings section, you will find an option called One-finger system gesture trigger range, with the following ranges: small, medium, big, and maximum. This setting defines the distance the finger needs to cover when performing one-finger system navigation gestures, such as swiping up from the bottom to go to Home.

Published in Tutorials

en.title: Apple Releases tvOS 27
en.summary: Apple has today released tvOS 27 for Apple TV 4K (2nd generation and later). According to Apple , tvOS 27 includes support for larger accessibility text sizes, high-resolution lossless audio in Apple Music, and a redesigned Podcasts app. More details should become available in the near future when Apple updates its "About Apple TV 4K and Apple TV HD software updates" Apple Support document. Unfortunately, we were not able to test tvOS 27 during the beta cycle; and thus we do not have any information on whether this release contains any changes to vision accessibility features beyond the added support for larger text sizes. If you have upgraded to tvOS 27, we would greatly appreciate hearing your experiences with the update. To install tvOS 27, go to the Settings channel, then look for the System section near the bottom. From here, look for Software Updates under Maintenance, then select Update Software and Download and Install. Wait for your Apple TV to download the update. Don't disconnect or unplug your Apple TV until the update completes.

en.title: Apple Releases iOS 27 and iPadOS 27
en.summary: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 are now available to the public. (Note: As spotted by AppleVis Community Member TJT 2001 , Apple has also released iOS/iPadOS 26.7 for those not wishing to upgrade to iOS 27.) This post contains Apple's Release Notes for iOS 27, as well as links to all of AppleVis' content related to these updates. Also included are instructions on how to install the update. iOS 27 Release Notes iOS 27 introduces the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, as well as new features to help parents create safe digital experiences for kids, and improvements that make iOS more responsive and delightful to use. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri that is more intelligent, knowledgeable, and capable. The next generation of Apple Intelligence also powers new features across apps that simplify the things you do every day, like editing images in Photos, communicating in Messages and Mail, and browsing in Safari. New parental controls and significant updates to Screen Time make it more intuitive and easy to use, so parents can feel confident that they're building the right digital experience for their child. And with improvements that span design, performance, connectivity, search, and more, the experience on iOS 27 has been refined and elevated, so it feels even better to use. Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max) A more capable and conversational version of Siri is rolling out to users. It helps you find what you need and get more done, drawing on capabilities like personal context understanding, app actions, onscreen awareness, and access to broad world knowledge. New voice experience offers more expressive and natural-sounding voices, and lets you customize expressivity and pace to make Siri more personal to you using powerful on-device models on iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro models and later. Dedicated Siri app provides an easy way to revisit an existing conversation or kick off a new one, and privately syncs conversations across your Apple products with iCloud. Siri mode in Camera integrates Visual Intelligence into the Camera app, letting you ask questions and take action with what's in front of you, like splitting a bill or looking up nutritional info for a plate of food. Write with Siri enables you to generate a draft from scratch, edit what you've written, or get feedback from Siri virtually anywhere you type. In Messages & Mail, Siri personalizes your writing style based on your relationships, and uses unique phrases and punctuation that you've previously used in your conversations with those people. Apple Intelligence across apps (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max) Photos. Spatial Reframing lets you adjust the composition of a photo after it was taken by virtually changing the camera position. Extend tool intelligently expands images beyond their edges with realistic infill, so you can straighten horizons, change aspect ratios, or add more space around a subject. Clean Up supports removing even larger objects, with more realistic, high-quality results, and you can choose between Fast mode for small blemishes or High Quality for more intricate edits. Safari. Organize by Topic uses Apple Intelligence to sort your tabs, analyzing webpages and automatically grouping similar tabs together. Notify Me can periodically check a webpage for updates, like price changes and item availability. Describe an Extension lets you create a custom extension using natural language to adjust your view of a website's content or formatting. All-new Image Playground uses a new generative model to make high-quality images in virtually any style, including photorealistic, lets you modify your images using touch and natural language, and lets you generate Lock Screen wallpapers and Contact Posters with personalized suggestions. Describe a Shortcut lets you use natural language to create a shortcut or refine an existing one. Home. Summarized activity notifications combine related alerts across accessories into a single notification. Video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video recordings summarize what's happening in a clip for eligible iCloud+ subscribers. Camera clip search lets you find specific moments from your HomeKit Secure Video cameras by searching in the Home app or Spotlight when on an eligible iCloud+ plan. Describe an event in Calendar lets you use natural language to create an event, and details like the time, location, invitees, and event title are filled in using Apple Intelligence. Suggestions in Mail help you take action based on the context of your emails, like getting directions to a restaurant you booked. Call Context in the Phone app understands when you're speaking to certain businesses and proactively surfaces relevant information from across your apps, like a confirmation code or a reservation number. Accessibility. VoiceOver enhancements include more detailed and contextual image understanding for photos, charts, and screenshots, a conversational experience that lets you ask questions about your screen or surroundings, and a new way to get answers fast with an Action button integration. An enhanced Magnifier experience offers conversational visual assistance for users with low vision, with a high-contrast interface and natural language app controls for zooming and other Magnifier functions. A smarter Accessibility Reader uses intelligence to provide better text cleanup and formatting, images and tables, on-demand summaries, and translation. Voice Control flexible inputs help you navigate your device with just your voice by describing elements on screen in your own words, like "tap the gear" or "tap the button in the top right". And more, including additional ways to create and modify Genmoji, automatic proofreading, and more accurate dictation using an on-device model on iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro models and later. Child Safety Improved setup experience for new child accounts lets parents choose the exact apps their kids can access when they set up an iPhone for their child. Ask to Browse gives parents the option to approve each new website before their child can view it. Expanded Communication Safety protections help intervene before children see gore or violent content in shared images and videos. Time Allowances help parents set boundaries around how long kids can use apps across Entertainment, Games, and Social Media apps, offering guidance based on expert research and tailored to each child's age. Schedules let parents choose which apps their kids can access at different points in their day and across weekdays and weekends. Redesigned Screen Time settings give parents at-a-glance information about how their kids use their devices, and controls to adjust access in just a few taps. System Improvements Liquid Glass refinements improve overall readability, and a new slider in Settings lets you personalize its appearance from ultra-clear to fully tinted . Faster performance in experiences across the system, including app launches, new photos loading in your Photos library, and AirDrop transfers. Improved search provides more relevant and comprehensive results in Spotlight, Photos, and Mail. Connectivity Assist enables more seamless transitions between Wi-Fi and cellular networks. And more improvements across apps and experiences, including enhancements to iCloud Shared Albums in Photos, Custom EQ for AirPods, support for perimenopause and menopause in Cycle Tracking in the Health app, and independent volume settings for Alarms and Timers. For information on the security content of Apple software updates, please visit: https://support.apple.com/100100 Some features may not be available in all regions or on all iPhone models. To learn more, please visit: https://www.apple.com/ios/feature-availability/ Usage limits may apply for some Apple Intelligence features. To learn more, please visit: https://www.apple.com/apple-intelligence Software updates, like this one, add new features and improvements that may affect performance and/or battery life. To learn more, please visit: https://support.apple.com/125039 AppleVis iOS 27 Content AppleVis has the following content available for iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: Blog Post: iOS 27 and iPadOS 27: A Summary of VoiceOver and Braille Issues and Improvements Blog Post: What's new in Accessibility in iOS 27 for Blind and DeafBlind Users , by Scott Davert Podcast: An Overview of the New VoiceOver and Braille Features in iOS 27 , by Michael Hansen Podcast: A Demonstration of the New Image Description Features in iOS 27 , by David Nason Podcast: A Demonstration and Walk-Through of the New Live Recognition Features in iOS 27 , by Levi Gobin How to Update iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 are available via Over-the-Air Update (Settings > General > Software Update), via Finder on a Mac with macOS Catalina or later, or via iTunes on a PC or Mac with macOS Mojave or earlier. Before updating, we strongly recommend making a full and complete backup of your device (either locally or in iCloud, depending on personal preference). This will ensure that, in the unlikely event that something goes wrong during the update process, you will have a current backup on hand in case a device restore becomes necessary. Also, if using OTA update, we recommend plugging your device into a power source for the duration of the download/installation process, so as to prevent the unlikely event of your battery going dead during the update.

en.title: macOS Golden Gate: New Features, Changes, Improvements, and Bugs for Blind and Low Vision Users
en.summary: Apple has today released macOS 27 Golden Gate to the public. As usual, we won’t cover the mainstream features here, concentrating instead on what's new and changed for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users. For an overview of the mainstream changes, we recommend this in-depth review by MacStories . Please remember to check the section about bugs to see if now is the right time to upgrade. There’s no harm in holding off a few weeks or months to let Apple address a problem you may find too disruptive to deal with. A note to braille users: the AppleVis team members doing testing with macOS Golden Gate are not heavy braille users. We have no information as to how well braille works in this release, so please keep this in mind when upgrading. If you are a braille user who has experience with Golden Gate, please share your findings in the comments to help the community. Changes for VoiceOver and Braille Users Improved Image and Screen Descriptions As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, VoiceOver in macOS Golden Gate can use Apple Intelligence to describe and answer questions about images or the current screen as it appears visually. Focusing on an image and pressing VO-Shift-L will describe the image, and you can find additional options, such as the ability to ask about an image, explore the image spatially, or describe the current screen, by pressing VO-Shift-R from anywhere in macOS. For added convenience, commands in this menu can be mapped in VoiceOver Utility > Commands. Note that while VoiceOver can describe and answer questions about what's on the screen, it cannot directly interact with elements like VOCR or Screen Recognition on iOS and iPadOS can. New Verbosity Options for Coding With macOS Golden Gate, you can customize how information such as line numbers, errors, and warnings are reported by VoiceOver in code editors like Xcode. These settings can be found in the new "Coding" tab in VoiceOver Utility > Verbosity. We do not currently know which code editors besides Xcode respect these settings. New "Actions" rotor for trackpad users With macOS Golden Gate, you can perform custom actions for the focused element, the same actions available in VoiceOver's Actions menu, using trackpad commands. To do this, enable trackpad commands if they're not already enabled, turn the rotor to "Actions," swipe up or down with one finger to select a custom action, and double-tap to activate it. "Ducking Amount" setting The "Ducking Amount" setting for determining how much other audio is ducked when VoiceOver is speaking, originally introduced with iOS 18 and iPadOS 18, has been brought to macOS with the release of Golden Gate. It can be found in VoiceOver Utility > Sound. Braille Improvements While it is not something we have been able to test, we are aware of the following improvements for braille users in macOS Golden Gate: As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, text field labels can now be shown in braille. You can change the format these labels are presented in, or hide them entirely, by going to VoiceOver Utility > Braille > Layout, and clicking Text Field Labels. As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, Braille Access in macOS Golden Gate supports plain text (txt) and portable document format (PDF) files. Improvements for Low Vision Users While it is not something we have been able to test, we are aware of the following improvement for low vision users: As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, content in Accessibility Reader can now be summarized and translated while retaining its original formatting on macOS Golden Gate. If you are a low vision Mac user, we would love to hear in the comments your experience and thoughts on this and any additional enhancements you encounter in macOS Golden Gate. Other Changes As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, the Aaron (English US), Arthur (English UK), Catherine (English Australia), Gordon (English Australia), and Martha (English UK) voices have been reintroduced with macOS Golden Gate. Like other voices, they can be used with Siri, as well as for accessibility functions like VoiceOver and Read & Speak. As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, subtitles for spoken dialog in videos where captioning is not already provided can be generated automatically in macOS Golden Gate. These can be turned on and adjusted when playing a video by clicking the "show legible media selection menu" button in the playback controls group. Writing Tools, previously accessed from many apps' Edit menus, as well as many text fields' context menus, is now accessed with VoiceOver by focusing on a text field and choosing "Show Writing Tools" from the Actions Menu. When toggling Cursor Tracking with VO-F3, its state is reflected in the "Mouse pointer:" popup menu in VoiceOver Utility. In prior versions of macOS, the state of Cursor Tracking was not reflected in this popup menu, which had the potential to confuse users. Change List In its support documentation, Apple lists the following changes for VoiceOver users in macOS Golden Gate: You can now turn off announcements that webpages send automatically, such as live scores, new messages, or status updates. Turn off Enable Web Announcements to silence announcements from a single area of a webpage or from the entire page. VoiceOver remembers your choice for that website, so the area stays silent the next time you visit. With the new Coding tab in the Verbosity category of VoiceOver Utility, you can choose whether VoiceOver announces line numbers, and whether it plays a tone or speaks a description when it encounters an error, a breakpoint, or the program counter. Bug Fixes and New Bugs for VoiceOver Users Below are lists of the bugs we believe to have been resolved in macOS Golden Gate, as well as new bugs introduced in this release. We strongly recommend that you read through the list of new bugs and any replies before updating, as this will allow you to make an informed decision on whether to install macOS Golden Gate or wait for a future release. While we are confident in the status of issues contained in this post, we do not claim that our bug list is definitive or that our assessments are infallible. Some issues may manifest only under specific conditions; this is all the more likely as software continues to add more features, and the number of available configurations and use cases in Apple's ecosystem continues to grow. You likely will not experience every bug that we list, and it is also likely that you will encounter issues that we did not experience during our own testing and daily use of macOS Golden Gate. To ensure the information here is as complete and accurate as possible, we would appreciate input from those who have installed macOS Golden Gate. Please confirm if you are encountering the same problems listed or if you have found workarounds. Please also let us know about any additional issues not mentioned here. Of course, it's even more important that you report any new bugs directly to Apple - they're already aware of the ones listed here. For an explanation of why and how to report bugs to Apple, see this post. Accessibility Bugs Resolved in macOS Golden Gate To the best of our knowledge, Apple does not routinely publish lists of bug fixes for VoiceOver or Braille across releases; thus, it is difficult to get a complete accounting of every issue that has been resolved or what fixes users can expect to see upon upgrading to macOS Golden Gate. With this in mind, our testing suggests that the following issues present in macOS Tahoe have been resolved or meaningfully improved in macOS Golden Gate: VoiceOver no longer speaks list items on webpages unreliably. Pauses between sentences are no longer extended when using VoiceOver's "Say All" command. It is once again possible to reply to a message in the Message app by selecting the "Reply" action in the Actions menu. The Actions menu for Messages in the Messages app no longer contains redundant tapback actions. New Bugs for VoiceOver Users in macOS Golden Gate Our testing suggests that the following bugs have been introduced in macOS Golden Gate: After clicking the “Proofread” button in the Writing Tools popover using VoiceOver, only the Next, Previous, and Close buttons are visible, with no way to view the specific changes made to the text. There is no way to open or redownload apps from the “Apps & Purchases” page in the App Store using VoiceOver, with each app conveyed only as a button with no actions available and nothing to interact with besides the app’s name. To redownload a previously purchased app, you must click the [app name] button to open the product page, and then click the "Redownload" button in the toolbar. The sections and buttons in Safari’s Page Menu lack accessibility labels. Interacting with a section and pressing VO-Space on an item (all of which are clearly labeled) works to activate the item; however, interacting with each item in a section reveals an unlabeled button. When playing audio or video, VoiceOver announces “system has new window” once the media has started playing. The identity and purpose of this window is not clear from this announcement, and no new items appear in the application or window chooser menus. Other Possible Bugs In addition to the bugs listed here, we strongly recommend you read this Megathread about the macOS Golden Gate RC , , as it contains a wealth of community reports about and experiences with the Release Candidate version of the software that may differ from our own. macOS Golden Gate release notes macOS 27 introduces Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence, new parental controls, and an expansive set of improvements that make your Mac even more responsive, reliable, and delightful. Experience the new Siri AI Introducing Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that’s more personal, more capable, and more conversational. It is integrated into Spotlight, so you can search for answers about almost any topic right from where you already search for things across your system. It can draw on personal context to find things across your messages, mail, photos, and more. And it can get things done across your apps, just by asking. Revisit and resume past conversations in the new dedicated Siri app, synced with iCloud across your Apple devices. Siri AI is rolling out to users, and you can get started by turning it on in Settings. Take action on what’s onscreen With Visual Intelligence, you can select a window of your screen and Siri can answer questions or take action with what’s onscreen, like adding events to your calendar. You can access Visual Intelligence with a dedicated keyboard shortcut — Command-Shift-Space. Powerful new ways to edit photos Use intelligent photo editing tools to reframe a photo after it’s been taken with Spatial Reframing or expand your shot with the Extend tool. And enhancements to Clean Up let you remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex. New tools to browse in Safari Automatically group your tabs into topics, so related pages are easier to find. With Notify Me, Safari can monitor pages for changes like price drops or restocks and alert you when it’s time to act. Describe an Extension lets you use natural language to create custom extensions, like adding a button to save your favorite recipes. Easily create Shortcuts using natural language With Describe a Shortcut, you can automate daily tasks with a simple description and all of the required steps are assembled on your behalf. For example, you can describe a shortcut to automatically text your partner when you’re headed home from work with an estimated arrival time based on traffic. Even more refined design Updates to Liquid Glass improve readability, and a new slider lets you customize how it looks, from ultra-clear to fully tinted. Uniform toolbars, edge-to-edge sidebars, and more detailed app icons further elevate the design. New child safety features Powerful new parental controls help parents manage what content their children see, who they can communicate with, and when they can access apps. Apple has today released macOS 27 Golden Gate to the public. As usual, we won’t cover the mainstream features here, concentrating instead on what's new and changed for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users. As on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, VoiceOver in macOS Golden Gate can use Apple Intelligence to describe and answer questions about images or the current screen as it appears visually. Focusing on an image and pressing VO-Shift-L will describe the image, and you can find additional options, such as the ability to ask about an image, explore the image spatially, or describe the current screen, by pressing VO-Shift-R from anywhere in macOS. Note that while VoiceOver can describe and answer questions about what's on the screen, it cannot directly interact with elements like VOCR or Screen Recognition on iOS and iPadOS can.

To do this, enable trackpad commands if they're not already enabled, turn the rotor to "Actions," swipe up or down with one finger to select a custom action, and double-tap to activate it.

Some issues may manifest only under specific conditions; this is all the more likely as software continues to add more features, and the number of available configurations and use cases in Apple's ecosystem continues to grow. You likely will not experience every bug that we list, and it is also likely that you will encounter issues that we did not experience during our own testing and daily use of macOS Golden Gate.

For an explanation of why and how to report bugs to Apple, see this post.

Experience the new Siri AI

Introducing Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that’s more personal, more capable, and more conversational. It is integrated into Spotlight, so you can search for answers about almost any topic right from where you already search for things across your system. It can draw on personal context to find things across your messages, mail, photos, and more. And it can get things done across your apps, just by asking. Revisit and resume past conversations in the new dedicated Siri app, synced with iCloud across your Apple devices. Siri AI is rolling out to users, and you can get started by turning it on in Settings.

Take action on what’s onscreen

With Visual Intelligence, you can select a window of your screen and Siri can answer questions or take action with what’s onscreen, like adding events to your calendar. You can access Visual Intelligence with a dedicated keyboard shortcut — Command-Shift-Space.

Powerful new ways to edit photos

Use intelligent photo editing tools to reframe a photo after it’s been taken with Spatial Reframing or expand your shot with the Extend tool. And enhancements to Clean Up let you remove distractions with better quality and more realistic infill, even when the scene is complex.

Automatically group your tabs into topics, so related pages are easier to find. With Notify Me, Safari can monitor pages for changes like price drops or restocks and alert you when it’s time to act. Describe an Extension lets you use natural language to create custom extensions, like adding a button to save your favorite recipes.

Easily create Shortcuts using natural language

With Describe a Shortcut, you can automate daily tasks with a simple description and all of the required steps are assembled on your behalf. For example, you can describe a shortcut to automatically text your partner when you’re headed home from work with an estimated arrival time based on traffic.

Time Allowances gives parents more flexible ways to manage kids’ time in apps across categories. Schedules manage which apps kids can access at different times of day and throughout the week.

es.title: Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 2 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 2 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 2 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es d26386e7ac3ac6d245c8adcfc82c07e9332278360af3396b69888b6b31e08d33. ¡Feliz lunes!

La entrada Ya disponible la segunda beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.title: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK)
en.summary: Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from…
en.body:
Published 13 September 2026 by Philip Heyse

Blind Accessibility Keyboard (BAK) is an Android keyboard for blind and low-vision users. Refined over many years together with blind users, it was rebuilt from the ground up in summer 2026: modern, faster, and adjustable in great detail.

Two ways to type, both letting you check a key before it is sent:

– Lift to Type: slide your finger over the keys, hear each one, and commit by lifting it – Double Tap to Type: the first tap reads the key, a second tap confirms it

1. Setup and settings:

Setup is guided step by step and confirms out loud when the keyboard is enabled and selected.

The settings screen is made for TalkBack: a switch and its label are read as one element, and sections announced with a “Section:” prefix.

Settings can be saved to a file and restored later. A session log can be exported or e-mailed if you need help.

2. Keyboard layouts:

264 layouts are included. For most languages you can choose between Simple (four rows), Fluent Flow (five rows with numbers), Fluent Flow with Cursor (plus cursor keys), PC (Ctrl, Alt and function keys), PC with Num Pad, and Robo Gear (familiar from standard smartphone keyboards).

Hold the space bar for the Quick Menu to switch layouts. The full list of languages is at the end of this text.

The app itself is translated into 30 languages, including Finnish, Malay and Urdu.

3. What you hear:

– Adjustable speed and pitch, with upper and lower case told apart by pitch – Choice of speech engine, with language, country and voice – Optional NATO alphabet, so “B” and “D” are never confused – Spoken names for punctuation, symbols and emoji – Announcements when the keyboard opens or closes, when you move between letters, numbers, symbols and emoji, and on Shift, Alt or Ctrl changes – Key click sounds in three styles, with adjustable volume – Vibration when typing and on gestures, each switchable separately

4. Voice input:

Start dictation with the microphone key or the Quick Menu, and choose between:

– Your device’s own dictation – A model running on your device: no account needed, works offline, though less accurate than the online options – Popular AI services, using your own API key, stored encrypted on your device only

5. Typing support:

– Auto-correct for many of the supported languages. One Backspace restores the original word. Never runs in password fields. – Text shortcuts: “brt” becomes “Best regards, Tom”. One Backspace undoes it. – Clipboard history above the keys. Tap an entry to insert it. – Your own keys for text you often need, such as your e-mail address – Optional capital letter at the start of a sentence – Adjustable delay and repeat speed when holding Delete or Backspace

6. Subscription:

BAK is funded by a small subscription. It costs less than the equivalent of one US dollar per month, and follows the local price level, so in many countries it is lower. It pays for ongoing work: fixing bugs, keeping up with new Android versions, and adding features. Before subscribing, you can try the keyboard in the test field on the app’s home screen. A subscription is needed to use it in other apps.

7. Help and contact: – https://bright-side.de/bak/ – ba * @ ********* de.de

The Help section in the app has the documentation, the mailing list, and a way to e-mail the developer.

8. Layouts for your language:

Arabic (also with French), Belarusian, Bengali, Bulgarian (Cyrillic, Latin, Phonetic), Canadian (also French, Multilingual), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English (UK, USA), French (France, Switzerland), German (Germany, Switzerland), Greek, Gujarati, Hebrew, Hindi (also InScript), Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian (Italy, Switzerland), Kannada, Marathi, Norwegian, Persian, Polish (also programmer), Portuguese (also Brazilian ABNT), Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Spanish (Spain, Latin America), Swedish, Tamil, Telugu, Turkish (F and Q), Ukrainian, Vietnamese.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The keyboard app was specifically designed for blind or visually impaired users.

es.title: Accesibilidad y Tecnología Vive el fútbol accesible con Movistar Touch en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
es.summary: Gracias a la colaboración entre la ONCE, Movistar y el Atlético de Madrid, las personas afiliadas podrán disfrutar de una experiencia más accesible e inmersiva durante los partidos de fútbol que se celebren en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
es.body:
Gracias a la colaboración entre la ONCE, Movistar y el Atlético de Madrid, las personas afiliadas podrán disfrutar de una experiencia más accesible e inmersiva durante los partidos de fútbol que se celebren en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Se trata de Movistar Touch , un servicio gratuito dirigido a aficionados con entrada para el encuentro, que permite seguir el desarrollo del partido mediante audiodescripción y una tableta háptica capaz de reproducir en tiempo real la posición del balón sobre el terreno de juego. Esta tecnología ofrece una nueva forma de vivir la emoción del fútbol y constituye un excelente ejemplo de cómo la innovación puede contribuir a derribar barreras y favorecer la participación de todas las personas.

Actualmente, el Riyadh Air Metropolitano es el único estadio de España que ofrece este sistema. Las personas afiliadas interesadas en utilizarlo deberán solicitarlo previamente enviando un correo electrónico a inclusion@atleticodemadrid.com , indicando el partido de LALIGA para el que desean adquirir entradas y hacer uso del servicio.

Es importante tener en cuenta que Movistar Touch dispone de un número limitado de unidades, por lo que se recomienda realizar la solicitud con la mayor antelación posible.

Esta iniciativa se enmarca en la colaboración que el Atlético de Madrid mantiene desde hace años con la ONCE y Fundación ONCE para seguir mejorando la accesibilidad de sus instalaciones y servicios, reforzando así su compromiso con un deporte más inclusivo y accesible para todos.

en.summary: It’s a busy and exciting time – it’s release time! Let’s dive in and see what’s new: NVDA 2026.2 Magnifier A new Beta already? Resetting to Factory Defaults NVDA 2026.2 NVDA 2026.2 has been released! This release includes a new built-in Magnifier feature, improvements to touch gestures and navigation, and expanded speech and braille capabilities.… Read More
en.body:
It’s a busy and exciting time – it’s release time! Let’s dive in and see what’s new:

NVDA 2026.2 has been released ! This release includes a new built-in Magnifier feature, improvements to touch gestures and navigation, and expanded speech and braille capabilities.

The Magnifier provides zoom and color filtering options to assist users with visual impairments. The Magnifier currently only supports full screen mode, with docked modes planned in a future release. Touch support has been significantly expanded with new pinch gestures and touch-based browse mode navigation for web content. You can now navigate between links, headings, form fields, and other elements using touch flicks.

Speech features have been enhanced with support for custom speech dictionaries that can be provided by add-ons and new dictionary entry types for more granular control. A new voice setting for OneCore voices was added to control pauses after punctuation. A new command allows repeating the last spoken information, with the ability to display it in a browsable message. The default gesture to repeat the last spoken information is NVDA+x , which can be changed in the Input Gestures dialog.

The braille display can now automatically scroll, and DotPad devices support multi-button combinations. The default gesture to toggle automatic scroll is NVDA+alt+k .

Liblouis has been updated with new Italian and Estonian braille tables. When resetting NVDA to factory defaults, an Undo button is now available to restore the previous configuration.

Download the new version from the NVDA 2026.2 release post (or by checking for updates from within NVDA).

As well as the article below, and a new extensive section on the magnifier in the User Guide, our “Basic Training for NVDA” module has been updated with a number of updates. Of particular interest is a new section on the magnifier, there is also a topic covering reading the last spoken information and other new and improved content. These new updates are currently only available in the electronic text version. You can purchase Basic Training for NVDA from our shop . If you have already purchased the module, you can download the new version with the Magnifier section from the downloads page after logging into your NV Access account .

We are very excited to incorporate a magnifier into NVDA for the first time. We have had a lot of comments from users who are excited for this feature, and we’ve had some questions too, so let’s cover off some of the things it can and cannot do, and why it is a useful addition to NVDA:

First Release Firstly, it’s worth highlighting that this is the first release of NVDA with a magnifier and so the features will improve over time. We try to ship NVDA features incrementally, keeping the initial design scope small and allowing for early user feedback. This allows us to grow the magnifier in response to user reaction. Currently NVDA only works as a full-screen magnifier. We plan to extend the options in future releases. Adding windowed / docked modes is a high priority once bugs are addressed and the full-screen mode is more polished.

What CAN the magnifier do? The magnifier has most of the features you might expect from such a feature: You can zoom in and out (from 1x up to 50x) The view will follow the mouse, keyboard focus, browse mode focus and NVDA navigator object and review cursor – user selectable You can pan the view with the keyboard, in configurable increments, or jump to the edges of the screen You can adjust the colours (normal, inverted or greyscale) You can choose how objects are tracked (Centred or relative to their position on screen) You can configure the keystrokes for the various functions There is a keystroke to briefly zoom out and show an overview of the screen

We have made a short demo of the magnification feature on our YouTube channel .

Should I change magnifiers? Particularly if you currently use another magnification solution, we very much encourage you to try out the NVDA magnifier. We are interested in your feedback, and particularly where you would like to see our feature improve.

If you already use Windows magnifier or another program, you can keep using it and it will continue to work with NVDA’s speech functions. Just as we don’t recommend having two screen readers running at once, we also wouldn’t recommend having NVDA’s magnifier AND another magnifier running at the same time.

If you do currently use Windows Magnifier, some of the reasons you may consider NVDA’s magnifier: It starts when NVDA starts (once you enable it) Configurable keystrokes Greyscale colour filtering mode Relative tracking mode Ability to follow NVDA’s object navigation and review cursor Keys to jump to edges of screen No settings window always on screen Ability to set your desired settings once and save to a portable copy you can use on any computer

If you use Windows magnifier in docked or lens mode, or some of the other features which haven’t yet made it into the NVDA magnifier in NVDA 2026.2, then you may wish to stay with Windows magnifier for now – but we do encourage you to try out the NVDA magnifier and let us know what you think.

Before we even got this edition of In-Process finished, to tell you all about 2026.2…. we ALREADY have a new beta? Of NVDA 2026.3 ? Yep! And I’m not going to talk about that yet – if you want to check it out, please head to the beta release announcement . What I did want to briefly mention, was how we came to have a new beta out, when the paint isn’t even dry on NVDA 2026.2?

Great question! And it comes down to how we develop software. Both our internal developers, and the community are constantly working on improving features, fixing bugs, and adding new things into NVDA. As a new piece of code gets incorporated into NVDA, it goes into an “Alpha” build – an early pre-release build with whatever has been changed recently. This lets our developers and our most dedicated testers try it out and give feedback. These come out almost daily (and sometimes several in one day). Because of the quick turnaround, we don’t share them on social media or here on the blog, but if you’d like to try them out, alpha builds are publicly available from the snapshots page . Be aware that they may not be as polished as the stable releases – though the process to test them out is identical.

So, generally a week after a stable release, we collate all the things which have been in alpha for at least a couple of weeks, and put them together into a “beta” release of the next version. While we may still have some features we are working on for later betas, as well any regressions or major issues discovered from the previous release, we can turn much of our development attention on towards the NEXT release.

So, if you ever find an issue with NVDA, the sooner you let us know, the sooner we can prioritise it and work on a fix as needed.

One of the perhaps less glamourous updates in NVDA 2026.2 is to a feature you hopefully don’t ever need to use.

“When resetting NVDA to factory defaults, an Undo button is now available to restore the previous configuration”

We’ve covered resetting NVDA to factory defaults previously , though it is worth being aware of. While something you hopefully don’t need, if you ever DO need it, it’s good to know it exists. With this new change, if you reset NVDA to factory defaults, a dialog appears advising “Your configuration has been reset to factory defaults. Choose OK to keep factory defaults, or Undo to restore your previous configuration”. This could be useful just in case you ever inadvertently activate the wrong item on the NVDA menu for instance, and may hopefully save you from needing go through setting up NVDA to your preferences again.

That’s all for this week, do update to NVDA 2026.2 if you haven’t already, and we’d love to hear your feedback on the new features – the magnifier of course, but also the other updates.

Ya están disponibles en nuestro catálogo nuevos productos tiflotécnicos, cuyas características principales se indican a continuación.

Bastón plegable ultraligero y muy fino, formado por seis elementos, muy cómodo para guardar en bolsillos y bolsos debido a sus reducidas dimensiones una vez plegado. Está realizado en aluminio de alta resistencia y pintado en blanco. Dispone de empuñadura de caucho ergonómica y contera giratoria.

Disponible en las siguientes medidas:

Contera giratoria con cáncamo para bastones Asturias 2

Enzo vive con su familia en Erizona, una preciosa montaña donde habitan muchas familias de erizos. Un día, la señora Aguja, una amiga de su madre, pasa por su madriguera a visitarlos. Al marcharse, quiere que Enzo le dé un beso y un abrazo, pero un enorme malestar se apodera de su cuerpecito, y acaba pinchándola sin querer. Por suerte, su mamá está ahí para reconfortarlo y contarle que es normal que no le guste que lo toquen sin permiso. Por eso, hay que aprender una palabra muy importante: EL CONSENTIMIENTO. Su mamá lo guiará a la hora de decidir si se siente cómodo o no con el contacto físico con otras personas.

Una historia entrañable con la que ayudar a tu peque a detectar y comunicar mejor sus sentimientos.
